blogs.title: Threats Without Stars: The Tenth Circuit's Strict Enforcement of the Persecution Standard
blogs.description: This post analyzes the *Jimenez v. Bondi* ruling on the substantive definition of "persecution," highlighting the Tenth Circuit's adherence to precedent finding that threats, even when combined with psychological distress and the experience of extreme danger, do not constitute sufficient harm if they do not result in physical injury or tangible restrictions on liberty. The analysis focuses on how this decision reinforces the high burden for physical refugee status in the 10th Circuit, citing specific 10th Circuit precedents like *Wiransane* and *Karki*.

blogs.title: The Nexus Paradox: Distinguishing Political Opinion from Professional Friction in Criminal Disputes
blogs.description: This blog post explores the Tenth Circuit's reasoning regarding the nexus requirement, specifically whether Petitioners' alleged harm stemmed from their political opinion (Liberal Party support) or a professional vendetta (investigating a criminal businessman). It discusses how the court applied the "central reason" test to distinguish between ideological animus and defensive retaliation, and the legal significance of proving that political affiliation was more than a tangential factor in a context involving narco-trafficking and criminal enterprises.

blogs.title: Reporting the Unreportable: The *Jimenez* Precedent on Exhaustion and the 'Unable or Unwilling' Standard
blogs.description: This article examines the legal doctrine surrounding the government's response to persecution, focusing on the necessity of seeking state protection from an individual claiming a government cannot protect them. It details the court's rejection of Petitioners' claim of a failing state based solely on the reactions of individual officers and rumors, reinforcing the rule that without evidence of actual police reporting or systemic demonstration of failure to act, a claimant cannot prove that the asylum-seeking government is "unable or unwilling" to protect them.
